title: Computer Networks
blurb: How data actually travels between machines -- essential backend engineering knowledge.

lessons.title: How computer networks work
objectives: Explain what a network is and describe LAN, WAN, and topologies at a practical level
Explain how LAN changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect LAN with WAN and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A computer network is simply two or more devices connected so they can exchange data. A LAN (Local Area Network) connects devices in one physical location, like an office or home; a WAN (Wide Area Network) spans a much larger area, connecting multiple LANs together -- the internet is the largest WAN of all.
examples:
# practical scale, smallest to largest:
# your home Wi-Fi = a LAN
# your company's offices connected across cities = a WAN
# a company's internal-only network = an intranet
# the whole public internet = the largest WAN, built of countless smaller networks
commonMistakes: Assuming 'the internet' and 'a network' are different kinds of things -- the internet IS a network, specifically a massive WAN connecting countless smaller networks together.
lessons.careerRelevance: This vocabulary is assumed baseline in any backend or infrastructure conversation.

lessons.title: Network devices: routers, switches, access points, modems & firewalls
objectives: Distinguish the roles of the core physical network devices
Explain how modem changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect modem with router and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A modem converts your internet provider's signal (cable, fiber, DSL) into a format your network can use. A router connects separate networks together and directs traffic between them -- typically your home network to the wider internet.
examples:
# a typical home setup, stacked:
# modem (talks to your ISP) -> router (directs traffic, often also acts as a firewall)
# -> switch (built into most routers, connects wired devices) -> access point (built in too, for Wi-Fi)
commonMistakes: Using 'router' and 'switch' interchangeably -- a router connects DIFFERENT networks together, while a switch connects devices WITHIN the same network.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding what each device actually does is essential for diagnosing real connectivity problems, not just naming the boxes.

lessons.title: The OSI model & the TCP/IP model
objectives: Describe both layered models and explain what encapsulation means
Explain how OSI model changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect OSI model with TCP/IP model and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The OSI model is a 7-layer conceptual framework for thinking about networking: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application -- from raw electrical signals up to the applications you actually use.
examples:
# encapsulation, simplified (sending an HTTP request):
# Application layer: your HTTP request data
# + Transport layer header (TCP: source/destination port)
# + Internet layer header (IP: source/destination IP address)
# + Link layer header (MAC: source/destination hardware address)
# -- each layer adds its own header before handing off to the layer below
commonMistakes: Trying to memorize OSI's 7 layers as if they're all equally used in practice -- real-world networking discussions center on the simpler 4-layer TCP/IP model far more often.
lessons.careerRelevance: Layered thinking is exactly how real network problems get diagnosed -- narrowing down WHICH layer is failing (is it DNS? TCP? the app itself?) is the core troubleshooting skill.

lessons.title: MAC addresses & IP addresses (IPv4, IPv6, public vs private)
objectives: Distinguish MAC addresses from IP addresses and identify private vs public IP ranges
Explain how MAC address changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect MAC address with IP address and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A MAC address is a hardware address burned into a network interface, used for delivery WITHIN a local network (the Link layer).
examples:
# MAC address: 3C:22:FB:4A:9B:1E -- identifies THIS specific network card, never changes
# Private IP: 192.168.1.42 -- only meaningful inside your home network
# Public IP: 203.0.113.5 -- how the outside internet actually reaches your network
commonMistakes: Assuming a device's IP address is permanent and unique like its MAC address -- private IPs are commonly reused across millions of different home networks, since they're never directly.
lessons.careerRelevance: Recognizing private vs public IP ranges instantly is a routine, practical skill in any backend or infrastructure debugging session.

lessons.title: Subnetting concepts (without the math)
objectives: Explain WHY networks are subnetted, conceptually, without doing subnet-mask arithmetic
Explain how subnetting changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect subnetting with subnet mask and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Subnetting divides one larger network into smaller, separate sub-networks -- this is a PURPOSE-driven decision, not a math exercise: it isolates traffic (a problem in one subnet doesn't flood the whole network), improves security (different subnets can have different firewall rules), and organizes devices logically (all servers in one subnet.
examples:
# conceptual example, no math needed:
# Subnet A (10.0.1.0/24): internal database servers -- no direct internet access
# Subnet B (10.0.2.0/24): public-facing web servers -- internet-accessible, isolated from the databases
# if Subnet B gets compromised, Subnet A isn't automatically exposed
commonMistakes: Thinking subnetting is purely an academic exercise in address math -- in real infrastructure, it's a deliberate security and organization decision.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding subnetting's PURPOSE (not the arithmetic) is what actually comes up when reviewing real infrastructure and security decisions.

lessons.title: Ports, sockets, TCP & UDP
objectives: Explain what a port and socket are, and contrast TCP with UDP
Explain how port changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect port with socket and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A port is a number (0-65535) identifying a specific service or application on a device -- port 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH. A socket is the combination of an IP address AND a port, uniquely identifying one specific connection endpoint.
examples:
# socket = IP address + port, e.g. 192.168.1.10:443
# TCP: web browsing, file transfer, email -- correctness matters more than raw speed
# UDP: live video calls, online gaming, DNS lookups -- speed matters more than perfect delivery
commonMistakes: Assuming TCP is always the 'better' choice because it's reliable -- for real-time media, UDP's lower latency is usually the RIGHT trade-off, since a slightly-lost frame beats a frozen.
lessons.careerRelevance: Choosing TCP vs UDP for a given feature is a real, practical backend architecture decision, not just trivia.

lessons.title: The TCP handshake, packets, frames & segments
objectives: Trace the 3-way TCP handshake and distinguish packets, frames, and segments
Explain how 3-way handshake changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect 3-way handshake with SYN and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before any data flows over TCP, both sides perform a 3-way handshake: the client sends SYN (synchronize, 'let's connect'), the server responds SYN-ACK (acknowledging, and requesting its own synchronization), and the client replies ACK (confirming) -- only then is the connection ESTABLISHED and ready for real data.
examples:
# 3-way handshake:
# Client -> Server: SYN
# Server -> Client: SYN-ACK
# Client -> Server: ACK
# -- connection now ESTABLISHED, data can flow

# same data, different names by layer:
# Transport layer: segment (has a TCP header)
# Internet layer: packet (segment + IP header)
# Link layer: frame (packet + MAC header)
commonMistakes: Using 'packet' as a catch-all term for any unit of network data -- in precise usage, packet specifically refers to the Internet-layer unit, not the Transport-layer segment or Link-layer.
lessons.careerRelevance: Tracing a handshake (or knowing it never completed) is one of the first things checked when diagnosing a real connectivity failure.

lessons.title: DNS, DHCP, ARP & ICMP (ping)
objectives: Explain what each of these four foundational protocols actually does
Explain how DNS changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect DNS with DHCP and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names (like example.com) into IP addresses computers actually use to route traffic -- often through a CHAIN of lookups (a CNAME pointing to another name, which finally resolves to an A record).
examples:
# DNS resolution can chain through multiple records:
# shop.example.com (CNAME) -> cdn.example.com (A) -> 93.184.216.34
# -- the final A record is what actually has an IP address

# ping uses ICMP echo request/reply to test reachability and measure latency
commonMistakes: Assuming DNS always resolves in one direct hop -- CNAME chains (a name pointing to another name) are common and add extra resolution steps before reaching the final IP.
lessons.careerRelevance: These four protocols cover an enormous share of real 'why can't I connect' debugging -- DNS and DHCP failures especially are extremely common in practice.

lessons.title: HTTP, HTTPS & TLS
objectives: Explain the HTTP request lifecycle and what TLS adds
Explain how HTTP changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect HTTP with HTTPS and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: HTTP is the application-layer protocol underlying almost all web traffic: a client sends a request (method, URL, headers, optional body), the server processes it and sends back a response (status code, headers, body).
examples:
# HTTP request lifecycle:
# 1. DNS resolves the hostname to an IP
# 2. TCP handshake establishes a connection (TLS handshake too, for HTTPS)
# 3. Client sends the HTTP request
# 4. Server processes it, sends back a response
# 5. Connection closes or stays open for reuse (keep-alive)
commonMistakes: Thinking HTTPS is just 'HTTP but encrypted' with no other guarantee -- TLS also verifies the SERVER'S IDENTITY via its certificate, protecting against impersonation, not just eavesdropping.
lessons.careerRelevance: Every backend service handles this lifecycle -- understanding exactly where DNS, TCP, and TLS each fit is essential for diagnosing slow or failing requests.

lessons.title: Routing, switching & NAT
objectives: Explain how routing decisions are made and why NAT exists
Explain how routing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect routing with routing table and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Routing is the process of choosing the best path for a packet to travel across multiple networks toward its destination -- routers maintain routing tables and make this decision hop by hop, not knowing the whole path in advance.
examples:
# NAT in action:
# Device A (192.168.1.10) and Device B (192.168.1.11) both share public IP 203.0.113.5
# the router tracks: 'the request going out on port 51000 belongs to Device A'
# so when the response comes back, it's correctly routed to Device A, not Device B
commonMistakes: Assuming every device on a home network has its own unique address as far as the internet is concerned -- NAT means the OUTSIDE world only sees the router's single public IP.
lessons.careerRelevance: NAT explains a huge share of real-world 'why can't an external service reach my internal server directly' questions.

lessons.title: Firewalls, proxies, load balancers & CDNs
objectives: Distinguish a forward proxy from a reverse proxy, and explain what load balancers and CDNs do
Explain how firewall changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect firewall with forward proxy and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A firewall filters traffic based on rules (allow/deny by port, IP, protocol). A forward proxy sits in front of CLIENTS, making requests on their behalf (hiding the client from the destination server).
examples:
# forward proxy: hides the CLIENT from the destination (e.g. a corporate proxy for outbound browsing)
# reverse proxy: hides the SERVER from the client (e.g. nginx in front of your actual backend)
# load balancer: routes each request to whichever of several backend servers should handle it
# CDN: serves a cached copy of your static assets from a server physically near the user
commonMistakes: Confusing forward and reverse proxies -- the direction of WHO is being hidden from WHOM is the entire distinction between them.
lessons.careerRelevance: Reverse proxies and load balancers sit in front of nearly every real production backend -- this is standard infrastructure vocabulary.

lessons.title: WebSockets, Server-Sent Events & network troubleshooting
objectives: Explain when to use WebSockets vs SSE, and name the core troubleshooting commands
Explain how WebSockets changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect WebSockets with Server-Sent Events and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Regular HTTP is request-response only -- the server can't push data to the client on its own. WebSockets open a persistent, two-way connection, letting either side send data at any time (used for chat apps, live collaboration, gaming).
examples:
# choosing WebSockets vs SSE:
# chat app (client sends AND receives) -> WebSockets
# live stock ticker (server only pushes, client never sends) -> SSE, simpler

# troubleshooting toolkit:
# ping example.com          -- is the host reachable at all?
# traceroute example.com    -- where does the path actually break?
# dig example.com           -- what does DNS actually resolve to?
# curl -v https://example.com  -- see the full request/response, including headers
commonMistakes: Reaching for WebSockets by default for any real-time feature -- if the client never needs to send data back over the same connection, SSE is simpler and sufficient.
lessons.careerRelevance: This troubleshooting toolkit is used daily by anyone doing real backend or infrastructure work -- fluency here is expected, not optional.

lessons.title: Routing protocols: OSPF & BGP fundamentals
objectives: Explain the purpose of OSPF inside a network and BGP between autonomous systems
Explain how OSPF changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect OSPF with BGP and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Routers need protocols to learn which next hop should carry traffic toward a destination. OSPF is a link-state interior routing protocol commonly used within an organization: routers share topology information and compute shortest paths.
lessons.example: A data-center or enterprise network may use an interior protocol such as OSPF to learn internal routes, while edge routers use BGP to exchange external prefixes with other networks. Application code normally does not run BGP, but infrastructure and network-automation roles need to reason about it.
commonMistakes: Calling BGP simply a shortest-path protocol.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.

description: How data actually travels between machines -- essential backend engineering knowledge.

quiz.q: What is a LAN?
options: A network confined to one physical location

quiz.q: What distinguishes a WAN from a LAN?
options: A WAN spans a much larger geographic area, connecting multiple LANs together

quiz.q: What does a router primarily do?
options: Connects devices within one network only
Connects separate networks together and directs traffic between them

quiz.q: How does a switch differ from an older hub?
options: A switch forwards data only to the specific intended device, rather than broadcasting to everyone

quiz.q: How many layers does the OSI model have?
How many layers does the TCP/IP model have?
What is encapsulation in networking?
options: Wrapping data in successive layer headers as it moves down the network stack

quiz.q: What is a MAC address used for?
options: Delivery within a local network at the hardware/Link layer

quiz.q: Which of these is a private IP address range?
Why does IPv6 exist?
options: It's faster than IPv4 for no other reason
IPv4's address space is running out; IPv6 provides vastly more unique addresses
IPv6 is only for private networks

quiz.q: What is the PRIMARY purpose of subnetting?
options: Isolating traffic, improving security, and organizing devices logically

quiz.q: What is a socket?
options: The combination of an IP address and a port, identifying a specific connection endpoint

quiz.q: What makes TCP 'connection-oriented'?
options: It requires no setup at all
It establishes a connection (the handshake) before sending data, and guarantees delivery

quiz.q: Why might UDP be preferred over TCP for live video calls?
options: Lower latency matters more than perfect delivery -- a dropped frame is better than a frozen stream

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the TCP 3-way handshake?
What is the difference between a packet and a frame?
options: A packet has an IP header (Internet layer); a frame has a MAC header added on top (Link layer)
Packets are only used in UDP

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
options: Translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses

quiz.q: What does DHCP do?
options: Automatically assigns an IP address (and settings) to a device joining a network

quiz.q: What does ARP resolve?
options: A known IP address to its corresponding MAC address on the local network

quiz.q: What protocol does the `ping` command use?
What does TLS add on top of HTTP to make HTTPS?
options: Encryption and server identity verification via a certificate

quiz.q: What does a routing table help a router do?
options: Decide the best next path for a packet toward its destination

quiz.q: Why does NAT exist?
options: To let many devices on a private network share one public IP address

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a forward proxy and a reverse proxy?
options: A forward proxy hides the client; a reverse proxy hides the server
Reverse proxies only work with UDP

quiz.q: What does a load balancer do?
options: Distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend servers

quiz.q: What does a CDN primarily improve?
options: Latency, by serving cached content from servers near the user

quiz.q: When is a WebSocket the better choice over Server-Sent Events?
options: When only the server ever needs to send data
When the client also needs to send data back over the same persistent connection

quiz.q: Which command shows the network path a packet takes, hop by hop?
Which command is used to directly query DNS records?
What would `netstat` or `ss` typically show you?
options: Active connections and listening ports on your machine

exercises.title: Trace a DNS resolution chain
exercises.prompt: Given that shop.example.com is a CNAME pointing to cdn.example.com, and cdn.example.com is an A record pointing to 93.184.216.34, what IP address does shop.example.com ultimately resolve to?
exercises.hint: follow the chain: CNAME to CNAME/A until you reach an actual A record

exercises.title: Classify an IP address
exercises.prompt: Is 172.20.5.1 a private or public IP address? Explain using the private IP ranges.

exercises.title: Diagnose a failed connection
exercises.prompt: A user reports 'the website won't load.' DNS resolves correctly, but the TCP connection to port 443 times out. What's the most likely cause, and what would you check next?
exercises.hint: likely a firewall blocking port 443, or the server/service isn't actually listening on that port -- check firewall rules and confirm the service is running and bound to that port

exercises.title: Choose TCP or UDP
exercises.prompt: You're building a real-time multiplayer game where occasional dropped position updates are acceptable, but delay is not. Would you choose TCP or UDP, and why?
exercises.hint: UDP -- lower latency matters more than guaranteed delivery for this use case

exercises.title: Diagnose a slow API response
exercises.prompt: An API request succeeds (200 OK) but takes 4 seconds. DNS resolved instantly and the TCP handshake completed quickly. Where would you look next, and why might a reverse proxy or load balancer be relevant here?
exercises.hint: the delay is likely happening at the application layer (slow backend processing) or a slow upstream dependency -- check reverse proxy/load balancer logs to see if the delay is in reaching the backend or in the backend's own processing time

projects.title: Network diagnostic CLI tool
projects.desc: Build a command-line tool that runs ping, traceroute, and DNS lookups against a given hostname and summarizes the results in plain language.

projects.title: Backend Network Diagnostic Tool (capstone-aligned)
projects.desc: Given a set of simulated network symptoms (DNS failure, TCP timeout, high latency, wrong HTTP status), build a tool that identifies the likely root cause and suggests next diagnostic steps.

interviewPreparation.q: Walk through what happens, step by step, when you type a URL into a browser and press enter.
interviewPreparation.a: DNS resolves the hostname to an IP address (possibly through a chain of CNAME records), a TCP connection is established via the 3-way handshake (plus a TLS handshake for HTTPS), the browser sends an HTTP request, the server processes it and returns a response, and the browser renders it -- each step is a place a real failure could occur, which is exactly why understanding each layer matters.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you diagnose 'the website is down' as a backend engineer?
interviewPreparation.a: Work through the layers in order: does DNS resolve? Does a TCP connection to the right port succeed? Does the server respond to HTTP at all, and with what status code? Tools like dig, curl -v, and checking whether the service is actually listening on its expected port narrow this down quickly, rather than guessing.

interviewPreparation.q: Why would you put a reverse proxy in front of your backend service instead of exposing it directly?
interviewPreparation.a: A reverse proxy centralizes TLS termination, can cache responses, load-balance across multiple backend instances, and hides your actual backend's address and implementation details from the outside world -- all without the backend service itself needing to handle any of that.

interviewPreparation.q: When would you choose UDP over TCP for a backend feature?
interviewPreparation.a: When low latency matters more than guaranteed, in-order delivery -- live video/audio, real-time gaming position updates, or DNS lookups themselves, where retrying quickly is preferable to TCP's overhead and retransmission delays.

interviewPreparation.q: Why can't an external service on the internet connect directly to a device on your private home network?
interviewPreparation.a: NAT means the outside world only sees your router's single public IP address -- there's no direct route to an internal private IP like 192.168.1.10 without something (a port forward, VPN, or similar) explicitly making that connection possible.

capstone.title: Backend Network Diagnostic Tool
capstone.description: Build a tool that, given a set of simulated network symptoms (DNS resolution status, TCP connection status, HTTP status code, and latency), identifies the most likely root cause and suggests a concrete next diagnostic step -- the same reasoning process a backend engineer actually goes through when a service reports 'can't connect' or 'it's slow.'
deliverables: A working diagnostic function that takes DNS/TCP/HTTP/latency signals and returns the most likely root cause, not just a generic error
Coverage of at least 4 distinct failure categories: DNS failure, TCP/port failure, HTTP-level failure (e.g. gateway timeout), and high-latency-but-otherwise-successful
A short written explanation of WHY each cause maps to its specific combination of signals, tied to the actual mechanics of DNS/TCP/HTTP covered in this course
At least one test case per failure category, verified against your own diagnostic logic
capstone.portfolioTips: This maps directly onto real on-call debugging work -- being able to say 'I built a tool that reasons through network layers the way I would during an actual incident' is a concrete, relatable signal for backend interviews.

industryUsage.usage: Operates one of the world's largest CDN and DNS infrastructure networks, where DNS resolution speed and reverse-proxy/load-balancing logic directly determine most of the internet's perceived performance.
Its VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) networking model is built entirely on the subnetting, routing, and NAT concepts covered in this course -- real cloud infrastructure work assumes this fluency.
Relies heavily on both WebSockets (for real-time chat) and UDP-based protocols (for voice/video), a direct real-world example of choosing the right transport protocol per feature.

careerApplications: Used by backend, cloud, DevOps/SRE, cybersecurity, and distributed-systems engineers to diagnose connectivity, DNS, routing, latency, and service-to-service communication problems.
